tool.name: CriticalHabitatFeature
tool.summary: Rescales a habitat suitability model by DISTANCE from a critical habitat feature -- a resource the species must stay near, such as escape terrain, perennial water, or rocky outcrops. You supply distance bands (in the raster's map units) with a percentage for each; every cell's suitability is multiplied by the percentage of the band its distance to the nearest critical-feature cell falls in. The workshop book's example: a riparian species keeps 100% of its score within 30 m of water, 80% from 30-60 m, 60% from 60-100 m, and 0% beyond 100 m. The critical feature can be a feature layer (selections honored) or a raster. END WITH A BAND OUT TO A VERY LARGE DISTANCE -- cells beyond your last band are left unchanged, with a warning. A modernized port of the CorridorDesigner Critical Feature tool. Needs no Spatial Analyst.
tool.usage:
WHY THIS TOOL EXISTS. Neither the geometric nor the additive combining method adequately handles a species that is ABSOLUTELY dependent on close proximity to one specific resource, and a standard habitat model for such a species can greatly overpredict its habitat. The workshop book's examples (section 2.6): bighorn sheep must stay within about 300 m of the steep slopes they use as escape terrain; many amphibians must stay near perennial waters for food, cover, and thermoregulation; many rattlesnakes and lizards must stay near rocky outcrops for cover. The remedy is to make suitability DECLINE WITH DISTANCE from the critical factor: isolate the critical feature as its own layer, then multiply the existing HSM by a percentage that falls off in distance bands. The book's riparian statement of it, exactly reproducible with this tool's bands: from 0-30 m of perennial streams the new HSM is 100% of the existing HSM; from 30-60 m, 80%; from 60-100 m, 60%; and anything beyond 100 m is not habitat at all -- 0%. The same mechanism works in reverse for a hazard the species must stay AWAY from: keep a small percentage in the near bands and 100% far away.
HOW EACH CELL IS SCORED. The tool computes every cell's straight-line distance to the nearest critical-feature cell, finds the first distance band containing that distance, and multiplies the cell's suitability by that band's percentage over 100. Bands must be ascending and are matched first-band-wins, so a distance on a shared boundary (exactly 30 in the example) takes the EARLIER band's percentage. NoData cells in the HSM stay NoData.
END WITH A HUGE FINAL BAND -- THE MOST IMPORTANT TIP. Cells farther than your LAST band's upper limit are left UNCHANGED (multiplied by 100%), and the tool warns with the count. That warning replaces genuinely wrong behavior in the original: its Reclassify step used the "DATA" option beyond the last band, silently multiplying the HSM there by the RAW DISTANCE in map units -- almost certainly never intended. Do not rely on either default: state your intent with an explicit final band out to a distance nothing can exceed, as the workshop book's own examples do -- "100 999999 : 0" for a species that cannot live far from the resource, or a wide 100% band for one merely favored near it.
DISTANCES AND BANDS ARE IN THE RASTER'S MAP UNITS. Meters on a UTM grid, feet on a State Plane feet grid -- and DECIMAL DEGREES if the HSM is in a geographic coordinate system, which makes distance bands nearly meaningless; the tool warns loudly there. Strongly consider projecting your data first. Distances are planar (straight-line on the grid), computed to the nearest critical cell by an exact Euclidean distance transform.
THE CRITICAL FEATURE INPUT, TWO WAYS. Give it a FEATURE layer (polygons, lines, or points -- perennial streams, mapped outcrops, digitized escape terrain) and it is rasterized onto the HSM grid; lines and points are burned with every cell they touch so thin features are not missed, polygons by cell center, and true-curve geometries (geodatabase buffer circles) are densified first so they do not collapse to their arc endpoints. An active MAP selection on a feature layer is honored -- only the selected features count, recorded in the messages and metadata (a dataset picked via Browse has no selection and uses all features). Or give it a RASTER -- every cell with data is treated as the critical feature (build one with a query: slope greater than 60 percent, a land-cover class); it is resampled onto the HSM grid if the grids differ. Either way the feature must overlap the HSM raster's extent, or every distance would be undefined and the tool stops.
THE OUTPUT IS THE SAME MODEL, MODIFIED -- AND ITS RECORD SAYS SO. The output carries the input HSM's own machine-readable analysis record forward with this rescaling appended as a post-processing step (feature, bands, selection note): the output is the SAME analysis product, just modified, and the Land Facet Data Report will describe the whole chain. An input with no record gets a fresh one started here.
CREDITS AND REFERENCES. The original CorridorDesigner HSM tools are by Dan Majka (dan@corridordesign.org, 2006-2007); these ArcGIS Pro versions are by Jeff Jenness and Dan Majka equally. Please cite: Majka, D., J. Jenness, and P. Beier. 2007. CorridorDesigner: ArcGIS tools for designing and evaluating corridors. http://corridordesign.org.

dialogReference.para: The habitat suitability model to rescale, on the 0-100 scale. The output keeps this raster's grid exactly, and the distance bands are in ITS map units -- the tool warns if those are decimal degrees (a geographic coordinate system), where distance bands make little sense.

The resource the species depends on. As FEATURES: polygons, lines, or points (perennial streams, outcrops, escape terrain); an active map selection is honored, lines and points are burned all-touched so thin features are not missed, and true-curve geometries are densified first. As a RASTER: every cell with data is the feature -- isolate it first with a query (a slope threshold, a land-cover class). Must overlap the HSM's extent.

param.name: bands
param.displayname: Distance bands (from, to, percent of score kept)

dialogReference.para: One row per band: from-distance, to-distance (both in the HSM's map units), and the percent of the suitability score kept there (0-100). Bands must be ascending; a distance on a shared boundary takes the earlier band. The workshop book's riparian example: 0 to 30 keeps 100, 30 to 60 keeps 80, 60 to 100 keeps 60, then 100 to 999999 keeps 0.

ALWAYS end with a band out to a very large distance. Cells beyond the last band are left unchanged (100%), with a warning -- the explicit final band is how you state what "far from the resource" means for this species.

The rescaled habitat suitability model, still on 0-100. A name is suggested from the input; a path in a folder without an extension is written as a GeoTIFF. The input's analysis record is carried forward with the feature and bands noted.

scriptExample.title: Critical Habitat Feature example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: The workshop book's riparian example: full suitability within 30 m of perennial streams, 80% to 60 m, 60% to 100 m, and no habitat beyond -- the huge final band making the beyond-range behavior explicit.
scriptExample.code:
import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages
arcpy.jenness.CriticalHabitatFeature( r"C:\project\hsm\Frog_HSM.tif", r"C:\data\hydro.gdb\perennial_streams", [[0, 30, 100], [30, 60, 80], [60, 100, 60], [100, 999999, 0]], r"C:\project\hsm\HSM_Critical_Frog_HSM.tif")
